newsitem.title: BELGIUM: North-south divide looms over future EU budget.
newsitem.headline: North-south divide looms over future EU budget.

text.p: A fight is looming between the European Union's rich north and its poorer members in the south about the budget needed to run the bloc after the turn of the century when it expands eastwards.

Spain set the stage for many months of budgetary wrangling last Thursday by refusing to commit itself -- thus blocking the issue -- on Europe's next multi-billion-Ecu research programme before it sees what the overall resources available will be after 1999.
What Spain fears most is that it will no longer receive the same amount of so-called structural funds -- grants from the EU to help the poorest regions catch up with the rest.

This could happen because the expected enlargement to eastern Europe will place even greater demands on the funds at a time when the richer countries are anxious to keep their payments to the central EU coffers under control.
The negotiations on the EU's budget ceilings after 1999 will not start until later this year, but Spain decided Thursday was not too early to state its case.

"Spain said a decision (on research) should depend on a broader decision on the future financial situation of Europe...I don't think that is acceptable, quite frankly," an irate Dutch Economic Affairs Minister Hans Wijers, whose country currently holds the EU presidency, said after a ministerial meeting on research issues.
Wijers's anger was seen as revealing more than just the normal frustration after a sterile day-long debate.

In a 15-nation club with deep wealth imbalances, it also meant that the Netherlands, home to consumer goods giants Philips and Unilever, had a lot more to gain from the bloc's research initiatives than its southern partners which do not have big industries with large research and development departments.
"Research programmes are the structural funds of the rich countries," a southern diplomat said.

Structural funds represent about 30 percent of the EU's annual spending of more than 80 billion European currency units ($92 billion). Spain receives about 27 percent of the total while Germany gets 23 percent, but it is Ireland which benefits the most when compared to its population.

Spain says its share is threatened by suggestions, including in the European Commission, that the funds should be refocused to combat unemployment especially in big cities and not just help regional development.

"It's alright to use money to fight unemployment. What is wrong is to think unemployment is concentrated in big cities because then you help mainly the rich countries where the big cities are," a Spanish diplomat said.
The EU has been struggling with high unemployment for about 10 years due in part to industrial decline.
With 18.3 million people out of work currently, a great number of them in France and Germany, the sentiment is growing that priorities should be shifted and scarce resources used where most needed.

There has also been much gnashing of teeth about recent company decisions to close operations in countries or regions not eligible for funds only to reopen or expand facilities in subsidised areas. This was the case of Renault and U.S. medical equipment firm Boston Scientific whose decision to leave Belgium prompted accusations of unfair competition.
EU leaders agreed in the early 90s to keep European central spending below 1.3 percent of the bloc's gross domestic product until the end of the century.

The Commission will present a proposal towards the end of the year on the new budget ceiling, which must cater for the first wave of new EU members -- possibly the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland in the beginning of the century.
It will also include proposals to reform the structural funds. That's when the real fight will begin.
